analysis.one_liner: Caps greenhouse gas pollution and requires utilities to supply a growing share of power from renewables.
analysis.headline: Introduced with 1 cosponsor on June 23, 2009, the bill was referred to 11 House committees and never received a vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have capped national greenhouse gas emissions and created a trading market for emission allowances, cutting capped emissions to 83% of 2005 levels by 2020 and 17% by 2050. It required electricity suppliers to draw an increasing share of power from renewables and efficiency (reaching 20% by 2021), funded efficiency standards, electric vehicles, and a smart grid, and returned auction proceeds and refunds to consumers, especially low-income households. At the same time, it gave free allowances to coal utilities, refineries, and energy-intensive manufacturers and funded carbon capture and nuclear loan programs. It was referred to 11 House committees and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income households, through consumer refunds and rebates funded by allowance auctions, an expanded earned income credit for childless workers, home-heating-oil and propane consumer allocations, rebates for low-income manufactured-home replacement, and efficiency programs for buildings and appliances. Workers gain through green-jobs training and climate-change worker adjustment assistance. The renewable energy, electric vehicle, and clean-technology industries gain a mandated market and federal programs. By design, coal-burning utilities, oil refiners, energy-intensive manufacturers, and nuclear developers also gain, through free allowances, a carbon-capture research corporation funded by utility assessments, and expanded loan guarantees.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers, clean-energy firms, and compensated fossil utilities

how_it_helps.text: Caps greenhouse gas emissions from covered sources and phases them down to 83% of 2005 levels by 2020 and 17% by 2050, with a federal registry to track emissions.
Requires large retail electric suppliers to meet a combined efficiency and renewable electricity standard rising from 6% in 2012 to 20% from 2021 through 2039, backed by tradable renewable credits.

Directs auction proceeds and allocations to benefit energy consumers, including climate-change consumer refunds, an energy refund program, a modified earned income credit, and allocations for home heating oil, propane, and kerosene consumers.
Provides rebates for low-income households, including replacement of manufactured homes and reimbursement for estimated purchasing-power losses under the new emission caps.
Creates green-jobs curriculum grants, expanded energy worker training, and climate-change worker adjustment assistance for workers displaced by the transition.
Strengthens efficiency across the economy: building codes and retrofit programs, appliance and lighting standards, industrial plant standards, and transportation efficiency goals.

analysis.who_pays: Fossil fuel producers and large industrial emitters, which must hold allowances (or offset credits) for their emissions, though the bill softens this with free allocations to refineries and trade-exposed industries. Electricity and fuel consumers may see costs passed through in energy prices, which the bill tries to blunt with consumer refunds and free allowances to local distribution companies. New program spending and the administrative cost of running a nationwide allowance market add to federal burdens.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large emitters; consumers via energy prices

drawbacks.text: Large amounts of the allowance value are given away free rather than auctioned — to energy-intensive trade-exposed industries, local distribution companies, merchant coal units, and refineries — which hands billions in value to incumbent polluters and weakens the price signal the cap depends on.
Covered entities can comply with offset credits instead of cutting their own emissions, so real-world pollution reductions depend on the integrity of offset verification.

The renewable electricity standard has cheap escape hatches: suppliers can pay $25 per missing credit, and most of the target can be met with claimed efficiency savings, with a governor's petition able to raise the savings share to two-fifths.

The bill creates a large new market in emission allowances and derivatives; even with CFTC oversight, settlement and clearing rules, and a limit on who can buy credit default swaps, it invites financial speculation in a commodity invented by the statute itself.

The bill relies heavily on carbon capture and sequestration, an unproven technology, to keep coal viable — setting performance standards for new coal plants while simultaneously building a federally backed research corporation funded by assessments on electricity consumers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is real but compromised: the bill would have put the first national cap on greenhouse gases, forced a shift toward renewables and efficiency, and returned significant money to low- and middle-income households. But it bought industry peace with free allowances, offsets, low compliance-cost escape hatches, and new subsidies for coal and nuclear, so a large share of the value created flows to the very companies being regulated, and ratepayers would fund carbon-capture research through assessments. An honest supporter would concede the cap is leakier and the giveaways larger than a pure climate bill would allow.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in 11 House committees and their subcommittees after its June 2009 introduction and was never brought up again; a nearly identical companion bill passed the House three days later but died in the Senate, and this bill expired when the Congress ended in January 2011.

narrative.text: Rep. Henry Waxman introduced the bill on June 23, 2009, for himself and Rep. Edward Markey; it drew 1 cosponsor.

It was referred to 11 House committees, led by Energy and Commerce, and in the following days was sent to subcommittees on energy, aviation, highways, railroads, water resources, and, in July, crime and terrorism.
No committee reported the bill, no vote was ever scheduled, and no further action appears in the record before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Carbon-intensive industries — coal-burning utilities, refiners, and energy-intensive manufacturers — are better off, because the bill never advanced and they never faced allowance costs. Ordinary people got no climate program, no consumer refunds, and no renewables mandate out of this bill.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Carbon-intensive industries that faced no new costs

for.name: Henry Waxman
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Sponsored and introduced the bill, his second vehicle that month for a comprehensive cap-and-trade program.

for.name: Edward Markey
for.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Energy and Environment
for.what_they_did: Joined Waxman as the bill's co-lead and original cosponsor.

for.name: Barack Obama
for.what_they_did: Pushed congressional Democrats throughout 2009 to pass comprehensive cap-and-trade climate legislation.

for.name: Nancy Pelosi
for.what_they_did: Brought the nearly identical cap-and-trade companion, H.R. 2454, to the House floor, where it passed 219-212 in June 2009.

against.name: Harry Reid
against.what_they_did: Never brought a comprehensive cap-and-trade climate bill to a Senate vote, and in 2010 abandoned the effort entirely.

against.name: 168 of 179 House Republicans

against.role: House Democrats who crossed party lines

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held on H.R. 2998 itself; the only recorded vote on the identical program came when the House passed its companion H.R. 2454 by 219-212, with 44 of 254 Democrats and all but 8 of 179 Republicans voting no.

industries.note: The bill caps their emissions but hands them free allowances through local distribution companies and merchant coal units, and creates a Carbon Storage Research Corporation funded by assessments on consumers of fossil-fired electricity. Their polluting business model is regulated yet subsidized to continue.

Refineries would pay for allowances as fuel producers but receive free allocations to offset the cost. The industry's interest ran against the cap, and the bill bought its acquiescence with compensation.

A federal mandate reaching 20% renewables and efficiency by 2021 creates guaranteed demand, tradable credits, a 3-credit multiplier for small distributed generation, and new transmission planning. Their growth is the mechanism of the bill's public benefit.

They face allowance costs but receive free allowances and a border-adjustment program to shield them from foreign competition. The bill locks in their free allocation as a permanent feature of any carbon market.

The bill creates a nationwide market in emission allowances and their derivatives under CFTC oversight, with clearing and settlement rules. Traders gain a new commodity to intermediate, with oversight the bill writes as it creates the market.

Subtitle I revises the energy loan guarantee program and creates a Clean Energy Deployment Administration to finance low-carbon projects, including nuclear. Their gain depends on the same low-carbon transition the public would benefit from.
The bill expands the definition of renewable biomass, broadens the renewable fuel standard, and lets landowners earn offset credits, opening new revenue streams for farms and forests.
